title: The first week: loved sinner
hook: the Exercises begin with honest sorrow held by mercy

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatian indifference: not coldness, but a preference held open. Your line was free to choose love. When something didn't go your way, what did love choose? Day one thousand one hundred forty-one.

Ignatius divides his Spiritual Exercises into weeks. A week, in his book, isn't seven days. He says plainly that some people will take longer over a week and some shorter, depending on what they're given. A week is a stage, a movement of the heart. And the first stage is the hard one. After the foundation, after the freedom, Ignatius asks the person praying to look honestly at sin: the angels' sin, Adam and Eve's, and then their own. That sounds grim. But the way he sets it up, the looking never happens alone. Today's word: the first week.

Ignatius doesn't ask anyone to stare at their failures in an empty room. He asks them to do it standing before Christ on the cross. And then to talk with him, the way one friend talks to another, and ask three plain questions. What have I done for Christ? What am I doing for Christ? What ought I to do for Christ? That's the frame of the whole week. The sorrow is real. Ignatius even asks for the grace of tears. But it's sorrow in front of one who, Christians say, already died for the one praying. Paul says it this way: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." While we were yet sinners. Not after we cleaned up. And somewhere in the first week, Ignatius has the person praying break into wonder. Why didn't the earth swallow me? Why have the sun and the stars, the fruits and the animals, the angels and the saints, all gone on holding me up? In Ignatius's telling, the answer is mercy, there the whole time. Jesus's story of the son who comes home puts it in one picture: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." The father runs before the son can say a word of his speech. That's the first week: a loved sinner. Both words true at once. Look back over this week and it's been a week of going inward. Teresa's castle, John's nada and his flame, Lawrence's stove, Ignatius's foundation and his freedom. And now this: in Ignatius's picture, the one who comes home finds the door already open.
screen: `WHAT HAVE I DONE, AM DOING, OUGHT I TO DO?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one wrong you've done, held by mercy. Sit and breathe. Let one thing come to mind, something real but not the heaviest thing you carry; this is two minutes, not a lifetime. Name it plainly, without excuses and without piling on. Then imagine it held, not thrown back at you. If you pray, you can bring it before Christ on the cross, as Ignatius did, and ask his three questions. If you don't, just hold it next to the picture of a father running down a road. The bell holds the time.
The first week. The opening stage of Ignatius's Exercises: honest sorrow for sin, held in front of a mercy that came first.
Your line: loved, as I am. Today, when you catch a mistake you've made, say the line under your breath before the usual lecture to yourself begins. Day one thousand one hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: In the Spiritual Exercises, whether in a long silent retreat or in daily life with a guide, the first week is spent praying over sin and God's mercy, often ending in a conversation with Christ on the cross and, for Catholics, sometimes in confession.

notes: Exercises §4 paraphrased: the weeks need not be seven or eight days each; some are slower, some quicker. Confirm. The total number of weeks is not stated, on purpose.

§53 colloquy paraphrased ('What have I done for Christ? What am I doing for Christ? What ought I to do for Christ?'); §54 'as one friend speaks to another'. Confirm. 'Three plain questions' is a count taken directly from §53.

§55 (asking for 'intense sorrow and tears for my sins') summarized as 'the grace of tears'; §60 cry of wonder (why the earth hasn't swallowed me, the heavens, sun, moon, stars, elements, fruits, birds, fish, animals sustaining me) simplified; confirm.
Week end (1135–1141): look-back names The seven mansions, Nada, The living flame, Pots and pans, Principle and foundation, Indifference.
Practice: deliberately gentle ('not the heaviest thing you carry'); confirm the tone is appropriate for listeners carrying serious harm.
howItsDone mentions confession 'for Catholics, sometimes' — confirm.

Editor (2026-10-02): dropped 'Here's the surprise' (same phrase as day 1131's hook); §60's list corrected (it names fruits, animals, angels and saints, not 'the people') and the answer 'mercy' attributed to Ignatius rather than asserted by the narrator; Luke 15:20–21 detail fixed: the father runs before the son says any of his speech, not merely before he finishes it (teach and myth).

Auditor (2026-10-02): 'sin: the world's, and their own' corrected to §50–53's order (the angels' sin, Adam and Eve's, then one's own); week look-back's closing line ('the room at the center was never locked', narrator asserting) tied to the father in Luke 15; carry's 'old speech' changed (repeated day 1129's practice phrase).
